messages.subject: Hierarchical (Conditional) Multinomial Logit Example
parts:
First, I would like to thank the Stan team for this most generous gift! I can only imagine the time and effort that has gone into this project. So thanks.

I have been playing around with Stan and the results are impressive. I started with a Hierarchical Linear Regression (as a response to Ian's earlier question on imbalanced panels) and the results were great.
(Blog pose here: www.sanjogmisra.com/blog/stan/)

Since then I have been playing around with a "real" example of a Hierarchical Multinomial Logit (Mixed Logit) as applied to a brand choice context (I'm in a business school!) 
I have attached files for those who are interested.  The code works and the chains generated converge very fast (realtive to BUGS/JAGS). Having said that, I have run into some issues that I was hoping others (the Stan team) could help with:

a) The compilation and sampling time is somewhat long (my comparison code in JAGS compiles and samples much faster but doesn't mix as well).  
b) At some points i get a "Non-Fatal" warning that the inverse Wishart draw is bad. 

Warning (non-fatal rejection): Error in function stan::prob::inv_wishart_log<i>(i): W is not positive definite (0)


c) While the chain converges fast in most cases, once in a while the sampling slows to a crawl and the resultant chain shows poor mixing (see attached pdf where chain #1 has poor mixing). Not sure why this happens. Sometimes the acceptance rates drop quite a bit even after the chain seems to have gotten to the "correct" parameter range. 

Any and all other thoughts are welcome. I am in the process of benchmarking Stan with JAGS, BUGS and available code in R but wanted to make sure I get the most efficient version before I do so. My guess is that I could vectorize my code better but cant seem to figure out how. 

Some Notes: 
I am using the -O3 flag.
I have tried using the multinomial distribution (rather than lp__) that doesn't help speed things up.
I have tried the multi_normal_cholesky (doesn't help speed)
tried and found that softmax function is not available in current version (remove from documentation?)

Looking forward to comments, ideas and suggestions.

Sanjog

Some Notes: 
I am using the -O3 flag.
I have tried using the multinomial distribution (rather than lp__) that doesn't help speed things up.
I have tried the multi_normal_cholesky (doesn't help speed)
tried and found that softmax function is not available in current version (remove from documentation?)

Looking forward to comments, ideas and suggestions.

etamu ~ multi_normal(mu_m_prior, mu_var_prior);

For any multivariate model where the covariance matrix is known (data), many of the density functions currently in Stan are inefficient because they effectively do a matrix inverse every time the log posterior function is evaluated. In this case, it is faster to calculate the inverse of mu_var_prior once (to get the prior precision matrix) and better still the transpose of Cholesky factor (t_L) of the prior precision matrix. Then, you can implement the log multivariate normal yourself with

v <- t_L * (etamu - mu_m_prior);
lp__ <- lp__ - 0.5 * dot_product(v,v);

Note that the determinant part of the multivariate normal is a constant so you don't need to worry about that (although it is different below). Also, in your case mu_m_prior is a zero vector, so you can just drop that.

In this line,

eta[h] ~ multi_normal(etamu,etavar);

etavar is an unknown parameter, so using multi_normal() is okay. However, multi_normal_cholesky() is faster if you parameterize the model in terms of the elements of the Cholesky factor of the covariance matrix (etavar). But, doing so presents a complication if you want to put an inverse Wishart prior on the covariance matrix because you have to handle the Jacobian yourself. Something like

parameters {
  real subdiagonals[(H * (H -1)];
  real<lower=0> diagonals[H];
  // other parameters
}
model {
  matrix[H,H] L_etavar;
  int counter;
  counter <- 1;
  for(i in 1:H) {
    for(j in i:(H - 1)) {
      L_etavar[i,j] <- subdiagonals[counter];
      counter <- counter + 1;
    }
    L_etavar[i,i] <- diagonals[i];
    for(j in (i+1):H) {
      L_etavar[i,j] <- 0.0;
    }
  }

  for(h in 1:H) {
    eta[h] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(etamu,L_etavar);
  }

  L_etavar * L_etavar' ~ inv_wishart((D+K-1), invR);
  // change-of-variables see "Absolute Jacobian Determinant of the Covariance Matrix Inverse Transform" in Stan manual
  for(h in 1:H) {
    lp__ <- lp__ + (H - h + 2) * log(diagonals[h]);
  }

  // rest of model ...
}

At the moment (this could change in the next version of Stan), multi_normal() and multi_normal_cholesky() are not vectorized, which is why you have to loop. This is regrettable because L_etavar gets inverted H times when it only needs to be inverted once. For the time being, you could get around this by parameterizing the model in terms of the Cholesky factor of the precision matrix rather than the covariance matrix. This resembles what we did above, except now you have to account for the determinant part of the (log) multivariate normal

parameters {
  real subdiagonals[(H * (H -1)];
  real<lower=0> diagonals[H];
  // other parameters
}
model {
  vector[H] v;
  matrix[H,H] L_etaprec;
  int counter;
  counter <- 1;
  for(i in 1:H) {
    for(j in i:(H - 1)) {
      L_etaprec[i,j] <- subdiagonals[counter];
      counter <- counter + 1;
    }
    L_etaprec[i,i] <- diagonals[i];
    for(j in (i+1):H) {
      L_etaprec[i,j] <- 0.0;
    }
  }

  for(h in 1:H) {
    v <- L_etaprec' * (eta - etamu);
    lp__ <- lp__ - 0.5 * dot_product(v,v);
  }
  lp__ <- lp__ + H * sum(log(diagonals)); // log-determinant part

  L_etaprec * L_etaprec' ~ wishart((D+K-1), R);
  // change-of-variables see "Absolute Jacobian Determinant of the Covariance Matrix Inverse Transform" in Stan manual
  for(h in 1:H) {
    lp__ <- lp__ + (H - h + 2) * log(diagonals[h]);
  }

  // rest of model ...
}

Also, note that your prior over L_etaprec * L_etaprec' = etaprec is now Wishart, as opposed to having an inverse Wishart prior over L_etavar * L_etavar' = etavar.

Hopefully, that makes sense and hopefully, that will all be less cumbersome soon.

Ben

On Saturday, September 22, 2012 9:24:04 PM UTC-4, tds151 wrote:
Why does one have to perform the jacobian increment, manually, when placing  LL' ~ inv_wishart() prior on for L, lower triangular?  Does Stan recognize L as a cholesky factor and therefore not perform the jacobian adjustment to the unrestricted sampling form?  this seem illogical.   how would one have any intuition that they would need to handle the jacobian, themselves?  in particular, for cov_matrix[D] fred;  with fred = LL'; I would not have to perform the adjustment for fred ~ inv_wishart();

This is certainly something that is unique to Stan. I believe the rule is:

1) If the LHS of a ~ is declared in the parameters block, then the user does NOT need to adjust lp__ with a log absolute Jacobian determinant because Stan will do it automatically if necessary. Similarly, if updating lp__ manually instead of using the ~ syntax, if the variable(s) that are contributing that that lp__ update are declared in the parameters block, then the user does NOT need to further adjust lp__ with a log absolute Jacobian determinant because Stan will do it automatically if necessary

2) If the LHS of a ~ is declared in the transformed parameters block or is declared as a local variable in the model block, then the user DOES need to adjust lp__ with a log absolute Jacobian determinant. Similarly, if updating lp__ manually instead of using the ~ syntax, if the variable(s) that are contributing that that lp__ update are declared in the transformed parameters block or the model block, then the user DOES need to further adjust lp__ with a log absolute Jacobian determinant.

When the user does this in the .stan file:

parameters{
  cov_matrix[K] Sigma;
}

The C++ code utilizes a Cholesky factor (L) --- even though L is not mentioned in the .stan file --- and comes out looking like:

Sigma = L * L.transpose();
lp__ += a log absolute Jacobian determinant

In other words, the user is utilizing the Cholesky factor without necessarily knowing it.

However, the C++ code is always utilizing unbounded primitive parameters that correspond to the parameters declared in the .stan file. The only exception is

parameters {
  real mu;
}

Since mu is unrestricted, there is no need to complicate things with a primitive parameter. In contrast,

parameter {
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}

is positive so the C++ will have something like

sigma = exp(sigma_primitive);
lp__ += a log absolute partial derivative

In other words, a Cholesky factor is the primitive parameter underlying a covariance matrix, just like sigma_primitive is the primitive parameter underlying sigma.

See the chapter of the manual on "Transformations of Variables" for more details.

Ben

On Saturday, September 22, 2012 10:26:43 PM UTC-4, tds151 wrote:
Thanks, Ben.   I now understand the distinction *when* the user needs to include the (log absolute determinant) jacobian adjustment.  that said, i don't understand why restricted parameters declared in the transformed parameters block if one specifies a distribution in the model block requires the adjustment.  If the restricted parameters in the transformed parameters block are a function of parameters in the parameters block (in fashion that obeys previously declared restrictions) and I place a distribution on the transformed parameters in the model block, then the sampling focus shifts to the transformed parameters.   I know one can't declare local parameters as restricted in the models block, but when may do so in the parameters block, right?  i ask these questions b/c if I understand the outlines of how the stan dev team thinks then i may write smarter .stan scripts.

It isn't really true that if you "place a distribution on the transformed parameters in the model block, then the sampling focus shifts to the transformed parameters". In your mind, you might be focusing on the transformed parameters, but from Stan's perspective the sampling is always done on the unbounded, unrestricted, primitive parameters (which the user never even sees). If Stan sampled directly from the transformed parameter space, the sampler (often) might get stuck in a region where the posterior evaluates to zero or is not defined. So, Stan samples from a parameter space where the posterior is defined everywhere and is non-zero everywhere. [In the future, Stan might have an option to bounce around in a transformed parameter subspace, but I doubt that will happen real soon]

Maybe you are thinking of a different example, but let me try to clarify using the AR1 example again. If your .stan file were

data {
  int<lower=1> K;
}
parameters{
  real<lower=0,upper=1> phi;
  real<lower=0> sigma_squared;
}
transformed parameters {
  cov_matrix[K] Sigma;
  // loops to fill in Sigma as a function of phi and sigma_squared
}
model {
  // informative prior on phi
  phi ~ beta(1,2);

  // informative prior on sigma_squared
  sigma_squared ~ exp(1);

  // should NOT have a prior on Sigma
  // should NOT have a Jacobian adjustment

  // some likelihood of the data as a function of Sigma
}

Alternatively --- although this makes little substantive sense to me --- you could do

data {
  int<lower=1> K;
  int<lower=K+1> df;
  matrix[K,K] scale;
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0,upper=1> phi;
  real<lower=0> sigma_squared;
}
transformed parameters {
  cov_matrix[K] Sigma;
  // loops to fill in Sigma as a function of phi and sigma_squared
}
model {
  // prior on Sigma with Jacobian adjustment
  Sigma ~ wishart(df,scale);  
  lp__ <- lp__ + SomeJacobianAdjustment;

  // should NOT have a prior on phi or sigma_squared

  // some likelihood of the data as a function of Sigma
}

In other words, a Wishart prior on the transformed parameter Sigma implies some prior on phi and sigma_squared (technically, it implies some prior on the primitive parameters underlying phi and sigma_squared but Stan automatically adjusts for the change-of-variables to phi and sigma_squared). The reason why I don't like this on substantive grounds is that it is almost completely opaque as to what a Wishart prior on the transformed parameter Sigma implies about phi and sigma_squared. But it is legal in Stan.

Conversely, I do like the first version which has informative priors on phi and sigma_squared (and no prior on Sigma or Jacobian adjustment) because I can easily understand what these two priors entail, even if I might disagree with them. In general, I would say that it is better for a model to put its priors on the parameters that compose a structured covariance matrix than to put a prior on the composed covariance matrix.

I would actually go further and say that --- if no other structure is attractive --- compose a covariance matrix as the product of a diagonal matrix of standard deviations, a correlation matrix, and a diagonal matrix of standard deviations. There are lots of choices of priors for standard deviations and Stan has a nice prior distribution for a correlation matrix called lkj_corr that takes a positive shape parameter, eta. If eta = 1, the prior is jointly uniform over all correlation matrices of order K, and to the extent that eta > 1, the prior has a sharper mode at the identity matrix of order K.

You see a lot of Wishart and inverse Wishart priors in the literature, but that is often because such priors are necessary for a Gibbs sampler. In Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, conjugacy is not relevant, so Stan users might as well use prior distributions that they believe or at least understand. With Wishart and inverse Wishart priors, the expectation is known but that's about it.

Ben

On Sat, Sep 22, 2012 at 9:59 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
On Saturday, September 22, 2012 9:24:04 PM UTC-4, tds151 wrote:
Why does one have to perform the jacobian increment, manually, when placing  LL' ~ inv_wishart() prior on for L, lower triangular?  Does Stan recognize L as a cholesky factor and therefore not perform the jacobian adjustment to the unrestricted sampling form?  this seem illogical.   how would one have any intuition that they would need to handle the jacobian, themselves?  in particular, for cov_matrix[D] fred;  with fred = LL'; I would not have to perform the adjustment for fred ~ inv_wishart();

This is certainly something that is unique to Stan. I believe the rule is:

1) If the LHS of a ~ is declared in the parameters block, then the user does NOT need to adjust lp__ with a log absolute Jacobian determinant because Stan will do it automatically if necessary. Similarly, if updating lp__ manually instead of using the ~ syntax, if the variable(s) that are contributing that that lp__ update are declared in the parameters block, then the user does NOT need to further adjust lp__ with a log absolute Jacobian determinant because Stan will do it automatically if necessary

2) If the LHS of a ~ is declared in the transformed parameters block or is declared as a local variable in the model block, then the user DOES need to adjust lp__ with a log absolute Jacobian determinant. Similarly, if updating lp__ manually instead of using the ~ syntax, if the variable(s) that are contributing that that lp__ update are declared in the transformed parameters block or the model block, then the user DOES need to further adjust lp__ with a log absolute Jacobian determinant.

When the user does this in the .stan file:

parameters{
  cov_matrix[K] Sigma;
}

The C++ code utilizes a Cholesky factor (L) --- even though L is not mentioned in the .stan file --- and comes out looking like:

Sigma = L * L.transpose();
lp__ += a log absolute Jacobian determinant

In other words, the user is utilizing the Cholesky factor without necessarily knowing it.

However, the C++ code is always utilizing unbounded primitive parameters that correspond to the parameters declared in the .stan file. The only exception is

parameters {
  real mu;
}

Since mu is unrestricted, there is no need to complicate things with a primitive parameter. In contrast,

parameter {
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}

is positive so the C++ will have something like

sigma = exp(sigma_primitive);
lp__ += a log absolute partial derivative

In other words, a Cholesky factor is the primitive parameter underlying a covariance matrix, just like sigma_primitive is the primitive parameter underlying sigma.

See the chapter of the manual on "Transformations of Variables" for more details.

Ben

In this case, the Jacobian is 1x1, so it is just the partial derivative of gamma with respect to sigma (which I totally messed up in my first attempt at a response). And thus
lp__ <-  lp__ + log(0.5 * pow(sigma, -0.5));
is the correct adjustment.

Chapter 26 of 1.0.1 reference manual covers this in the most detail. If this were a real model that utilized both sigma and tau for some reason, I would declare tau as the parameter and sigma as the transformed parameter (or as a local parameter within the model block) if you wanted to place an informative prior on gamma.

That is still intended to be a factual statement. Also, as Jeff points out, the simplest non-trivial example of a multivariate change-of-variables is

https://code.google.com/p/stan/source/browse/src/models/basic_distributions/wishart2x2.stan

Ben
